name: NeetCode
tagline: Curated LeetCode problem roadmaps with video walkthroughs and pattern-based courses.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is the thinnest part of the product: a problem list, a progress checkbox, an embedded video player. What people actually pay for is the curation, the NeetCode 150 and its pattern groupings, plus the explanations that make a hard problem click in nine minutes. An agent can build you a beautiful spaced-repetition tracker in an afternoon and it will be empty. You can point it at the public problem lists and even at the free videos, but the moment you want editorial solutions, hidden test cases, or the specific ordering that makes the roadmap work, you are rebuilding years of one person's teaching judgment. Build the tracker, keep paying for the content if the content is what you need.
coreLoopDIY: A local practice tracker that stores the problem list you enter, schedules reviews with spaced repetition, and runs your Python solutions against test cases you write yourself.
requirements: Node 20+ and Python 3 with pytest installed locally
You supply the problem list and any tests you want to run against
A judge to actually grade solutions still means writing your own test cases
whatYouLose: The video explanations, which are most of the value
The curated ordering and pattern grouping that turns 150 problems into a syllabus
Editorial solutions in multiple languages with complexity analysis
Hidden test cases and a real judge, so your tests only catch what you thought of
Any sense of where you stand relative to other people grinding the same list
moatNotes: The roadmap and the videos are one person's explanatory work, not a feature set. Nothing in a code generator produces that.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the bottleneck in interview prep was never tracking which problems you finished, it was understanding why the two-pointer solution exists at all. NeetCode sells compression of that understanding, plus the psychological relief of a finite curated list instead of three thousand random problems. A self-built tracker solves the part that was already easy. If you already know the patterns and just want a review scheduler, build it; if you are learning, you are paying for teaching, not software.
notes: The tracker is a weekend build; the teaching is not. The moat is a curated 150-problem roadmap and the video explanations that go with it.
prompt:
Build a local-first coding interview practice tracker. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/practice.db
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only

Data model:
- problem: id, title, url, difficulty (easy|medium|hard), pattern (free text tag like "two pointers"), notes (markdown)
- attempt: id, problem_id, date, outcome (solved|hint|failed), minutes, reflection text
- review schedule derived from attempts using SM-2 style spacing: solved pushes the interval out, hint holds, failed resets to 1 day

Pages:
- /  today's queue: problems due for review, sorted by due date, with a big "start" button that records a start time
- /problems  full table with filters by pattern, difficulty, and last outcome; inline add form; CSV import from a file with columns title,url,difficulty,pattern
- /problems/[id]  problem detail: link out, my notes in markdown, attempt history, a code editor pane (plain textarea with monospace font, no fancy editor) that saves my latest solution per problem per language
- /stats  attempts per week, solve rate by pattern, streak counter. Recharts, nothing exotic.

Local judge:
- A directory ./solutions/{problem_slug}/ holding solution.py and test_solution.py
- An API route POST /api/run that shells out to `pytest` in that directory with a 10 second timeout and streams stdout back to the UI
- Be explicit in the README that the tests are mine to write and that this is not a real judge with hidden cases

Explicitly out of scope: scraping any problem site, bundling problem statements or editorial solutions, user auth, deployment, mobile app.

Seed the db with an empty schema and three example rows. Put nothing in .env since nothing needs a secret; if I later add an LLM hint feature, read OPENAI_API_KEY from .env and no-op cleanly when it is missing. Write a README with setup, the spacing algorithm in plain English, and the honest limitation that this tracks practice but does not teach patterns.
